subject: Creativity
title: TRIZ: The Theory of Inventive Problem Solving
description: A quick, practical guide to TRIZ: The Theory of Inventive Problem Solving.

hook.text: A Soviet engineer analyzed 400,000 patents and found that all inventions use just 40 recurring principles.

buildup.text: Genrich Altshuller created TRIZ in 1946 — a systematic method for invention based on patent analysis.

discovery.text: TRIZ identifies 'contradictions' in design — when improving one feature worsens another — then resolves them.

twist.text: Altshuller developed TRIZ while imprisoned in a Soviet gulag. He tested ideas on fellow prisoners' engineering problems.

climax.text: Samsung used TRIZ to generate 50+ patents per year, transforming from a copycat manufacturer into a global innovator.

punchline.text: All inventions follow 40 patterns. You don't need to be a genius — just know.

quiz.question: How many recurring inventive principles did Altshuller identify in TRIZ?

details.summary: TRIZ is a systematic innovation methodology based on analyzing 40,000 patents to identify 40 universal inventive principles. Developed by Genrich Altshuller, it provides specific problem-solving strategies matched to specific types of technical contradictions.
details.whyItMatters: TRIZ proves that invention follows patterns. Instead of relying on random inspiration, engineers and innovators can systematically select proven solution principles matched to their specific problem type.
takeaways: TRIZ identified 40 inventive principles from patent analysis
Problems are framed as contradictions to be resolved
Each contradiction type maps to specific solution principles

faq.question: What is a TRIZ contradiction?
faq.answer: A TRIZ contradiction exists when improving one parameter worsens another. For example, making a structure stronger often makes it heavier. TRIZ provides specific principles for resolving each type of contradiction without compromise.

faq.question: Is TRIZ only for engineering?
faq.answer: TRIZ was developed for technical innovation, but its principles have been adapted for business, management, and service design. The core idea that problems contain inherent contradictions that can be systematically resolved applies broadly.
